paras: The whipping of a Black woman at Blue Ridge Springs, Virginia, took place on a Saturday night in late July 1903, when a party of white men beat an unnamed Black woman accused of insulting the wife of a local physician, Dr. Early. The papers treated it as notable less for the whipping than for what followed: Black residents were reported buying guns and ammunition in Roanoke, whites armed, and dispatches warned of a threatened race riot.

According to a Scripps-McRae dispatch from Roanoke, the woman had entered Dr. Early's yard some nights earlier and insulted his wife. The Associated Press version said only that she had insulted a white woman "in the absence of her husband." Both accounts gave this accusation as fact, and no version from the woman herself appears in the coverage.

On the Saturday night, which fell shortly before the dispatches of July 27 and 28, "a number of white men" took the woman and, in the Scripps-McRae wording, "whitecapped" her, giving her "a sound beating." The Associated Press described the attackers as "a party of white men" and said she was whipped; none of them was named.

The whipping angered Black residents of the neighborhood, who were reported to be arming themselves and "making threats." The Associated Press said several Black men came to Roanoke on July 27 and bought guns and ammunition, while a Roanoke hardware merchant told the Scripps-McRae correspondent that "a large number" had done so. A telephone message that night said the whites were also armed, and the Scripps-McRae dispatch described them as "heavily armed with pistols and guns."

No report of arrests, of any official action, or of how the threatened clash ended appears in the coverage. The last items found, printed July 30 and 31, still described trouble as threatened rather than reporting any fighting.

The Associated Press story, datelined Roanoke, July 27, ran on July 28 in papers from New York and Washington to Birmingham, Savannah, St. Paul and Omaha. Smaller papers in North Carolina, Virginia and South Carolina carried it over the next two days, and the Fredericksburg Free Lance printed it under the heading "Race Riot Imminent." A separate Scripps-McRae telegram, with the names and the hardware merchant's claim, appeared in the Stark County Democrat of Canton, Ohio, as "On Verge of a Race Riot."

Headlines centered on Black residents taking up arms, such as "Negroes Buy Arms" in the Raleigh News & Observer and "Blacks Armed and Trouble Is Feared" in the Birmingham Age-Herald. The Omaha Daily Bee's subhead read "Negress Is Whipped. Thus Stirring Colored Blood with Desire for Reprisals," and several papers stated the insult in their headlines as the cause of the whipping. Virginia's Alexandria Gazette and South Carolina's Yorkville Enquirer reduced the story to one-sentence items in news roundups.
No coverage of the episode in the Black press was found.

The accounts differ in detail: the Associated Press placed the trouble "near Blue Ridge" and spoke of "several blacks" buying guns, while the Scripps-McRae dispatch and the Alexandria Gazette named Blue Ridge Springs and Dr. Early's household, and the Scripps-McRae account cited "a large number" of buyers on the word of a hardware merchant.

reader.title: Whipping of a Black woman at Blue Ridge Springs, Virginia
bases: A party of white men whipped a Black woman at night over an alleged insult, which the Scripps-McRae dispatch called being 'whitecapped' (A2, A13).

The Associated Press wire (A2, A10) and a separate Scripps-McRae dispatch (A13) agree that white men whipped a Black woman near Blue Ridge Springs for an alleged insult to a white woman and that both races then armed; the Alexandria Gazette (A3) adds the same core facts.

accounts.label: Associated Press wire (Roanoke, July 27)
accounts.gist: Several nights earlier a colored woman was whipped by a party of white men for insulting a white woman in her husband's absence; Black residents armed and bought guns in Roanoke, and a telephone message said whites were armed.

accounts.label: Scripps-McRae dispatch (Roanoke, July 28)
accounts.gist: The woman entered Dr. Early's yard and insulted his wife; on Saturday night she was 'whitecapped' and beaten by white men; a hardware merchant said a large number of Black men bought guns, and whites were heavily armed.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the AP text nearly verbatim under headlines stressing armed Black residents ('Negroes Buy Arms', 'Blacks Armed and Trouble Is Feared', 'Race Riot Imminent').
Headlines and the wire stated the insult as fact and cast the whipping as the cause of Black anger, with the Omaha Bee writing of 'Colored Blood' stirred to 'Reprisals'.
Virginia and South Carolina papers carried the story as short state or news-digest items.

A Saturday night just before July 27-28, 1903 (about July 25).
Blue Ridge Springs (near Blue Ridge); Roanoke is the dateline and where arms were bought.
County not stated in the coverage.
A party of white men, unnamed.
A night band of white men ('whitecapped').
At least 12 papers on this episode, July 28-31, 1903; the July 12 item is not about it.

info: A Saturday night shortly before July 27-28, 1903 (the Scripps-McRae dispatch of July 28 says 'Saturday night'; the AP wire of July 27 says 'several nights ago'); the alleged insult came 'several nights' before the whipping.
Near Blue Ridge / Blue Ridge Springs, Virginia; dispatches datelined Roanoke.
An unnamed Black woman ('colored woman', 'negro woman').
Accused of insulting a white woman in her husband's absence (AP); of entering Dr. Early's yard and insulting his wife (Scripps-McRae).
'A party of white men' / 'a number of white men'; none named.
No report of how the threatened clash ended was found.
